name: Methadone
summary: A drug with a lethal mismatch built into it: the effect lasts about six hours, the drug lasts about thirty, and the half-life varies between people by a factor of seven. Dose for how it feels and you accumulate for days. Most methadone deaths happen in the first two weeks of treatment, to people taking it as directed.
mechanism: A long-acting full mu agonist, which is why it holds withdrawal at bay for a full day and blunts the effect of other opioids taken on top. It is also an NMDA antagonist, which may be why it retains effect where tolerance to other opioids is high. Its very long half-life is what makes it useful for maintenance and dangerous during induction.

oral.note: Well absorbed, with bioavailability ranging from 40% to nearly 100% between individuals — a twofold uncertainty before the half-life variability is even considered.

pathways.name: EDDP
pathways.note: The main inactive metabolite and the one measured in treatment monitoring.

pathways.name: Unchanged renal
pathways.note: Renal excretion rises when urine is acidic.

effect_levels.label: 100 µg/L — generally regarded as the lower end of a holding dose
1000 µg/L — toxicity reported in non-tolerant individuals

risk: Put four daily doses on the timeline and watch the trough rise each day. That climb is the induction death: the drug accumulates for about five half-lives — up to a week — while the subjective effect from each dose has worn off long before the next is due. Taking extra because it 'stopped working' is the mechanism.

The half-life range here is 8 to 59 hours. Two people on the same dose can end up at completely different steady-state levels, and there is no way to tell which you are in advance. This is why methadone is titrated slowly.
It prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes, particularly above about 100 mg daily or alongside other QT-prolonging drugs.
CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors shift the level substantially — some antibiotics, antifungals, antiretrovirals and anticonvulsants. A new prescription can change a stable dose into an unstable one.
Naloxone's effect is far shorter than methadone's, so reversal of a methadone overdose requires prolonged observation, not a single dose.

sources.text: Eap CB, Buclin T, Baumann P. Interindividual variability of the clinical pharmacokinetics of methadone. Clin Pharmacokinet. 2002;41(14):1153-93.
